headline: Applying an artistic style to a selected object
intro: I built an application for selecting an object in a photo and applying an artistic style to it. The selected area changes while the surrounding image stays the same.
context: University of Michigan · Computer Vision course project · Sept–Dec 2022
role: I proposed the idea and led the design, implementation, model comparisons, and integration into the final application.

hero.alt: Six-second before-and-after sequence showing the original black swan transitioning into the AdaAttN segmented style-transfer result.
hero.caption: A before-and-after sequence made from course-report images. It shows the selected swan changing style; it doesn't show the model running.

metrics.label: AdaIN stylization time
metrics.note: Mean of 600 transfers; excludes segmentation and compositing

question.title: Selecting the area to change
question.text: The application uses clicks to select an object and refine its mask, which marks the area to edit. It then combines the styled object with the original background.

steps.title: Select with clicks
steps.text: Positive and negative clicks guide FocalClick toward the object and away from areas to leave out, so users can adjust the mask without tracing the whole outline.

steps.title: Compare the models
steps.text: I compared AdaIN, AdaAttN, IEContraAST, and PAMA using ArtFID, then measured stylization time in a separate experiment.

steps.title: Keep the original background
steps.text: The mask determines which pixels come from the styled image and which come from the original.

gallery.alt: Progress presentation screenshot of a click-based object-selection interface, generated mask, and tower-styling example.
gallery.caption: The selection interface, a mask, and a styling example from the progress presentation. I finished combining them into one application later.
gallery.credit: Original team presentation, 1:35 · DAVIS / WikiArt imagery

finding.title: Comparing ArtFID and speed
finding.text: AdaIN had the shortest measured stylization time. AdaAttN had the lowest ArtFID, at 27.419 compared with AdaIN's 27.955. Lower ArtFID is better on this measure.

charts.title: Stylization time by model
charts.subtitle: Report measurements · 600 transfers per model · lower is faster

details: The timings cover stylization only, excluding segmentation and compositing. The report doesn't specify the hardware or measure how long the full application takes.
The 1,000-input evaluation and timing chart come from the course report. The progress presentation shows an earlier experiment with different scores.
